candidates.attacker_control: Query parameters of a GET request to the OAuth 2.0 authorization-response URL (`/oauth2/authorize/code/{clientAlias}?error=...&error_description=...`). The filter matches the path with no HTTP-method restriction and Consumes the `error` parameter before any `state`/authorization-request lookup, so the attacker fully controls the string that becomes the exception message (paragraph: ErrorResponseAttributesConverter -> OAuth2Error.toString()).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified the normal authorization-code path DOES validate state and redirect URI (AuthorizationCodeAuthenticationProcessingFilter lines 182-205), so this is not a missing-state/CSRF claim on the success path; verified the login page cannot be reflected into directly because DefaultLoginPageGeneratingFilter.matches() compares the exact URI (`/login?error`), so a plain `/login?error=<payload>` does not render (payload must first be stored through the failure handler); verified the exception is session-scoped, not just request-scoped (SimpleUrlAuthenticationFailureHandler lines 104-117); verified the default failure URL `/login?error` is registered by AbstractAuthenticationFilterConfigurer (lines 363-376) and that the generated login page is addable in the default WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter flow (WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter lines 199-214 + DefaultLoginPageConfigurer.configure); confirmed no HTML escaping helper (HtmlUtils/TextEscapeUtils) is used anywhere in the rendering path, and no CSP header is set by default (HeaderWriterFilter writers set X-Content-Type-Options/X-Frame-Options/HSTS/Cache-Control only); checked that apps with a custom login page/failure handler/entry point are unaffected.
candidates.impact: Script execution in the application's origin whenever the built-in login page is shown (including in the repo's own oauth2login sample configuration). A successful hit also passes through unsuccessfulAuthentication(), which clears and removes the session security context, so a logged-in victim is first logged out; the injected script then runs on the login page and can keylog/phish credentials, exfiltrate page content and CSRF tokens, and act in the origin as that (anonymous) session, i.e. credential theft and client-side compromise. The same unvalidated error path also lets anyone force a failed login/logout of a victim (CSRF-style DoS).
candidates.prerequisites: Application uses `oauth2Login()` (or another login mechanism whose failure message embeds user input) with the framework-generated default login page, i.e. no `loginPage(...)`/`failureUrl(...)`/custom `AuthenticationEntryPoint` (this is the configuration of the repo's own samples/boot/oauth2login sample). Victim must be lured to the crafted callback URL (one GET); the failure handler creates the session and issues a 302 to the exact `/login?error` URL that the login-page filter matches. No authentication or CSRF token is required because the triggering request is a GET and the CSRF matcher ignores GET/HEAD/TRACE/OPTIONS.
candidates.root_cause: The OAuth 2.0 authorization-response error path treats request parameters as trusted error data: ErrorResponseAttributesConverter reads `error`/`error_description`/`error_uri` directly from the HTTP request, AuthorizationCodeAuthenticationProcessingFilter throws OAuth2AuthenticationException whose message is `OAuth2Error.toString()` (attacker text), SimpleUrlAuthenticationFailureHandler stores the exception in the session, and DefaultLoginPageGeneratingFilter writes `ex.getMessage()` into the `/login?error` page via string concatenation with no HTML escaping or output encoding. The error branch is executed before any state/redirect validation, so no prior session state or CSRF token is needed.
candidates.title: Cross-site scripting on the default login page via attacker-controlled OAuth 2.0 error parameters
candidates.trace: 1) attacker link: /oauth2/authorize/code/x?error=e&error_description=<payload> (AntPathRequestMatcher matches, no method check). 2) AuthorizationCodeAuthenticationProcessingFilter.attemptAuthentication calls errorResponseConverter.apply(request) first; ErrorResponseAttributesConverter returns attacker text (lines 39-52). 3) A new OAuth2AuthenticationException(oauth2Error, oauth2Error.toString()) is thrown (lines 128-131); OAuth2Error.toString() = "[code] description" (OAuth2Error.java 70-73); state/redirect checks in assertMatchingAuthorizationRequest (lines 194-205) are never reached. 4) AbstractAuthenticationProcessingFilter.unsuccessfulAuthentication delegates to the default SimpleUrlAuthenticationFailureHandler(/login?error) (AbstractAuthenticationFilterConfigurer.updateAuthenticationDefaults lines 367-369); saveException() stores the exception under WebAttributes.AUTHENTICATION_EXCEPTION in the new session (lines 110-115) and redirects to /login?error (line 91). 5) The browser follows the redirect; DefaultLoginPageGeneratingFilter matches the exact URI /login?error, reads ex.getMessage() (lines 199-201) and appends it unescaped into the HTML (line 216), executing the attacker's markup in the application origin.
candidates.unverified: The end-to-end browser execution, CSP/browser behavior, and any real deployment configuration were not executed or tested (no code was run and no tests exist in this snapshot). I could not consult upstream fix history or CVE data (per review constraints), so I cannot confirm whether this behavior was later patched upstream or is the benchmark's intended ground truth; the finding is a source-traced lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.
candidates.weakness_type: Cross-site scripting (CWE-79); improper neutralization of attacker-controlled input in generated HTML

coverage_summary: get_source_scope reports 1340 model-visible files, 0 excluded by size/name/symlink filters, with binary-like files skipped by the reading tools; get_relation_scope reports a complete index over all 1340 files (9191 symbols, 15648 calls, 14278 edges) with no missing files and explicitly no SAST/reachability proof, which I treated as navigation hints only. Depth-reviewed: web (context repos/filters, CSRF, login/logout/remember-me/basic/digest/switch-user, firewalls, request matchers, request cache, headers, SavedRequest), config (annotation web/http configurers, DefaultLoginPageConfigurer, AbstractAuthenticationFilterConfigurer, oauth2 login configurers, WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter defaults), oauth2-client/oauth2-core (redirect filter, processing filter/provider, state generator, session repository, Nimbus token exchanger/user service, registration classes), cas (filter/provider/service details/cache), openid, ldap (encoder/template/search), acl (JDBC lookup/services), core (authentication providers, access interceptors/voters/expression handling, token services, reactive authorization), messaging (CSRF interceptor, matchers), crypto (key generation/encryptors/BCrypt), taglibs, and webflux (filters, authorization manager, context repository). Sampled only: aspects, remoting, data, docs, itest, most non-oauth2 sample apps and parts of the XML namespace parser code.
limitations: Source-only review: no build, tests, scanners, or exploit execution were performed, and the snapshot contains no test sources, so no test-based confirmation of any finding.

No access to upstream fix history, advisories, or CVEs per the review constraints, so the candidate cannot be matched to a known patch; confidence in it being the intended ground-truth issue is moderate, not high.
The relation index is syntactic/navigational only and does not prove data flow, reachability, or exploitability; every edge used in the candidate trace was re-verified against source text.

Configuration dependence: the XSS requires the framework-generated default login page (no custom login page/failure handler/entry point) plus an OAuth2-login-style flow; custom-login-page deployments are not affected.
Modules/files reviewed only by sampling (aspects, remoting, data, itest, docs, most sample apps, parts of the XML namespace config) could contain additional issues that this review does not cover.

rejected_leads.lead: CAS open redirect / service-URL tampering (DefaultServiceAuthenticationDetails, CasAuthenticationFilter service handling)
rejected_leads.reason: The snapshot already builds the CAS service URL from the configured `casService` URL (protocol/host/port) plus the request URI (DefaultServiceAuthenticationDetails lines 55-63) instead of trusting request scheme/host; the historical URL-hardening is present and no attacker-controlled host flow was found.

rejected_leads.lead: OAuth 2.0 login CSRF via missing state validation
rejected_leads.reason: State and redirect-URI checks are present for the authorization-code callback (AuthorizationCodeAuthenticationProcessingFilter lines 182-205). The error branch skipping those checks is real but is the enabler of candidate cand-1, not a separate high-impact candidate; its standalone impact is a forced authentication failure/logout.

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultHttpFirewall hardening gap (no StrictHttpFirewall, no backslash/encoded-character blacklist, allowUrlEncodedSlash option)
rejected_leads.reason: No concrete request that would bypass a protected pattern was traced; upstream later added StrictHttpFirewall as defense-in-depth. Treated as a hardening opportunity, not a demonstrated vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: Open redirect through AbstractAuthenticationTargetUrlRequestHandler's configurable `targetUrlParameter` (unvalidated absolute/`//host` URL)
rejected_leads.reason: The parameter is null by default and must be explicitly enabled by the application; DefaultRedirectStrategy is unchanged from upstream. No attacker-controllable redirect in the default configuration.

rejected_leads.lead: UserDetailsRepositoryAuthenticationManager compares raw passwords with String.equals and has no PasswordEncoder support
rejected_leads.reason: Very early reactive/in-memory helper in this snapshot; no evidence it is wired into the default servlet or WebFlux security configuration, and the comparison itself is a direct password check rather than a bypass.

rejected_leads.lead: samples/boot/insecure (and samples/xml/insecure) intentionally disable security / ship demo credentials
rejected_leads.reason: Explicitly insecure sample applications used for demonstrations; not a vulnerability in the reviewed framework code.

rejected_leads.lead: Additional escaped/reflected-data sinks (taglib AuthenticationTag, oauth2 client-name links on the login page, DefaultSavedRequest redirect URL)
rejected_leads.reason: Taglib output is escaped by default; login-page client names/URLs come from trusted registration configuration, not request input; DefaultSavedRequest reflects the current request's own URL and matches upstream behavior.

summary: Repository is a Spring Security 5.0.0.BUILD-SNAPSHOT tree (mid-2017, Spring Boot 2.0.0.M1) with 1340 model-visible source files across core/web/config/oauth2-client/oauth2-core/cas/openid/ldap/acl/messaging/taglibs/crypto/webflux/remoting/samples. I traced attacker-controlled input through the OAuth 2.0 authorization-response handling into the framework's generated default login page and found a cross-site-scripting (CWE-79) candidate: the OAuth 2.0 error path accepts unauthenticated request parameters (`error`, `error_description`), places their text in an `OAuth2AuthenticationException` message, has the failure handler persist that exception in the victim's HTTP session, and the default login page then writes the exception message into HTML without any escaping. All hops were verified in source (filter -> converter -> provider/error -> failure handler -> session -> login page). This is the strongest distinct issue I found; several other plausible leads were checked and rejected (details below).
